title: Qullamaggie Breakout and the Kell Cycle
teaches: The Qullamaggie breakout and Kell's cycle as we trade them: a leader rests 10 to 40 sessions in a tightening range with rising lows, surfing its rising averages, the buy is a market order as price trades over the base high, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, 1-3% preferred, 3.5% good, up to 5%, and past 5% we wait for a tighter trigger, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail; Kell's cycle then says wait, buy, sell into strength or get out, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: An orderly pullback and consolidation with higher lows and tightening range in the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: an orderly consolidation with higher lows and a tightening range.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price “surfs” the rising 10- and 20-day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: during the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day.

facts.quote: just look at the daily chart and enter when the stock is starting to break out.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: on the daily chart, enter when the stock starts to break out.

facts.quote: This method can also be traded by anticipating the breakout but I don’t find it as effective and more skill and experience is needed.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: anticipating the breakout is less effective and needs more skill.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: The rest of the position should be trailed with the 10- or the 20-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: trail the rest with the 10- or 20-day average.

facts.quote: 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages guide us through the intermediate-term trend
facts.claim: Kell: the 10 and 20-day EMAs guide the intermediate-term trend.

facts.quote: When the 10-day exponential moving average is below the 20-day, there is no reason to be long the stock.
facts.claim: Kell: with the 10-day EMA under the 20-day, there is no reason to be long.

facts.quote: The Reversal Extension is not necessarily a playable setup but more of a change in mindset.
facts.claim: Kell: the Reversal Extension is not necessarily a playable setup.

facts.quote: Many traders mistakenly believe the Wedge Pop is simply about crossing the moving averages.
facts.claim: Kell: a Wedge Pop is not simply a crossing of the averages.

facts.quote: Enter on a strong price bar with increased volume when the stock breaks through the pivot.
facts.claim: Kell: enter on a strong bar with increased volume through the pivot.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback refers to the first time the stock price retests its moving averages after a strong upward move
facts.claim: Kell: the EMA Crossback is the first retest of the averages after a strong upward move.

facts.quote: But always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in before making your trade.
facts.claim: Kell: wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.

facts.quote: The Base n’ Break is another pullback into the moving averages after the EMA Crossback.
facts.claim: Kell: the Base n' Break is another pullback into the averages after the EMA Crossback.

facts.quote: once you get two Base n’ Breaks, you should realize you are late in the intermediate-term cycle
facts.claim: Kell: after two Base n' Breaks you are late in the intermediate-term cycle.

facts.quote: The proper buy area is through the pivot into new highs.
facts.claim: Kell: the buy area is through the pivot into new highs.

facts.quote: The Exhaustion Extension is a euphoric blowoff price movement well above the 10-day moving average
facts.claim: Kell: the Exhaustion Extension is a blowoff well above the 10-day.

facts.quote: Start to get defensive when there is “air” between the low of the day and the 10EMA.
facts.claim: Kell: get defensive when there is air between the day's low and the 10 EMA.

facts.quote: The Wedge Drop happens when the market trades back below the moving averages after a strong rally, known as an Exhaustion Extension.
facts.claim: Kell: the Wedge Drop is a trade back below the averages after an Exhaustion Extension.

facts.quote: It may only be 3-4% above the moving averages but that was too much.
facts.claim: Kell, on his losers: 3-4% above the averages was too much.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; skip if the honest stop does not fit.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit and only moves up.

facts.quote: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account)
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before earnings; hold through only if up 5R.

facts.quote: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day, unless it is a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: Bull markets only: a Green market reading.
facts.claim: Card: bull markets only, a Green market reading.

facts.claim: Card: the first base after the move is the A+ case.

facts.quote: A sideways consolidation after the move with at least two rising swing lows.
facts.claim: Card: a sideways consolidation with at least two rising swing lows.

facts.quote: The range tightens: the average daily range of the last 5 sessions is below the average of the whole consolidation.

facts.quote: The consolidation runs 10 to 40 sessions.
facts.claim: Card: the consolidation runs 10 to 40 sessions.

facts.claim: Card: a base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth.

facts.claim: Card: closes hold above the rising 20-day EMA through the base.

facts.claim: Card: no volume rule; volume raises the grade only.

facts.claim: Card: the daily-chart version is a trade above the consolidation high.

facts.quote: No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report; hold through a report only if up 5R.

facts.claim: Card: a few cents under the breakout day's low, the day's low so far at an opening-range buy.

facts.claim: Our stop sits within 5% of the buy: 1-3% preferred, 3.5% good; past 5%, wait for a tighter trigger. Kullamagi's own cap is the stock's ADR.

facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

walkthroughs.title: CRSP, November 2019: the shortest base that counts
steps: Big move first, then a short rest. CRSP, 2019: an earnings reaction kicks off a 47% run.
Then 10 sessions of rest, only 14% deep. That's short and shallow next to the run before it.
November 12 it clears 52.28 on 3.1x volume. Buy at market, 52.35. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 51.21.
A 2.2% stop, where we like it. A close back inside the base means it failed. Instead, 3R in 1 day.

walkthroughs.title: HWM, May 2025: a steady name after an earnings gap
steps: This one's steady, not a rocket. HWM, 2025: a large name with a 43% run and an earnings gap.
Then 12 tight sessions in a 17% band. Calm, sideways, holding its gains.
May 15 it clears 161.58 on 1.5x volume. Buy at market, 161.59. Stop a few cents under the low, 158.95.
Just a 1.6% stop. A close back in the base says it failed. This one took 7 days to 3R.

walkthroughs.title: CPRI, December 2020: quiet volume, still a breakout
steps: CPRI, 2020. A 59% run in a month, then 11 sessions with each low a little higher than the last.
It's 21% deep, but its rising short-term averages never let go. That's a stock resting, not breaking down.
December 3 it clears 38.00 on only 0.8x volume. Buy at market, 38.01. Stop a few cents under the low, 37.37.
Volume only raises the grade, so a quiet break still gets bought. Stop 1.7%, and 3R came in 5 days.

questions.q: This is the day before the breakout. How would you describe the rest it just made?
choices: Flat lows with wide, loose swings
questions.why: Sideways, with higher lows, and the range getting tighter. That's the rest Kullamagi buys, and it's what you want to see here. Each pullback stops a little higher than the last, so buyers keep stepping in sooner. The daily swings shrink as it goes, so sellers are running out. And the lows ride the rising 20-day instead of breaking it. When a rest like that clears its high, there's very little overhead to stop it.
questions.lesson_line: Higher lows and tighter swings into the high. That's a rest worth buying.

wrong.Drifting down through the 20-day: This one held its rising 20-day. A drift down through it means it's losing its trend.
wrong.Sideways, lower lows, getting wider: Lower lows and wider swings mean sellers are getting stronger. That's a stock coming apart, not resting.
wrong.Flat lows with wide, loose swings: Loose and sloppy. I want the swings to shrink into the break, not stay wide.

questions.simple: Sideways with higher lows and tighter swings. Buyers step in sooner each time, and that's the rest we want.

reasons: Two agreeing facts: Kullamagi's page and UCT's card

questions.q: A stock with an RS rating of 62 builds a picture-perfect base. It's still not a breakout we take.
questions.why: Right, we pass. We only buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A 62 means plenty of stocks have done better than this one. A clean base on a laggard is still a laggard. When the money comes in, the leaders are where the big moves happen. So check the RS rating before you fall for the base.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders first. Check the RS rating before you fall for the base.
questions.simple: True. A great base on a weak stock is still a weak stock, and we only buy leaders here.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On the breakout day our card wants the close above the 50-day and ___-day simple averages.
questions.why: 200. On the breakout day the close is above the 50-day and the 200-day, with the 50-day above the 200-day. Our rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 50, above the 200, and the 50 over the 200.
questions.simple: The close must be above the 50-day and 200-day averages, with the 50-day above the 200-day.

deeper.trap: Two ideas sit in this one line. No longs below the 200-day simple average is the rulebook line, with one exception, a parabolic long. The 50-day above the 200-day is how the card reads a leader's stack. Mixing them up makes the rule sound stricter or looser than it is.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
the 50-over-200 half is the card's reading, not the rulebook's

questions.q: The base high is marked and your alert is set. Price trades through it at 10:40. How do you get in?
choices: Market order as it goes through
Limit order a bit over the high
Half now, half on a retest
Wait for the close above it
questions.answer: Market order as it goes through
questions.why: Market order, right as it trades through. That's how we buy everything. A limit order can leave you watching it run without you. Waiting for the close is worse. By then it's often a few percent higher, and your stop under the low of the day sits further away. So you set the alert the night before, and when it hits, you buy. Full size, one price, one stop.
questions.lesson_line: Alert set the night before. It trades through, you buy at market.

wrong.Limit order a bit over the high: A fast break can jump right over your limit. Then you're out of a good trade, or chasing it.
wrong.Half now, half on a retest: We buy the full size at one price with one stop. No starter half, no buying more on a retest.
wrong.Wait for the close above it: We never buy the close. We buy the trigger while it's happening, during the day.

questions.simple: Buy at market as it trades through the high, so you get the break and not a chase later.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, market orders)

questions.q: You bought the break. The low of the day so far is 24.10. Your stop goes a few cents under it, around 24.05.
questions.why: Yep. The low of the day, the LOD, is where this breakout is wrong. If buyers can't hold today's low, the break failed. Put the stop right on the low and a quick wick can tag you, then reverse. A few cents under gives it that little bit of room. Kullamagi does the same: his stop is always the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the LOD. That's where the break is wrong.
questions.simple: True. The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, where the break is proven wrong.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62, A4)

questions.q: The stock's ADR is 2.9%. The low of the day puts your stop 3.5% away. You can still take this breakout.
questions.why: You can. Kullamagi caps his stop at the stock's ADR, its average daily range. We judge the stop by how far it sits from the buy instead. 1-3% is what I like, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is fine. So 3.5% is a trade. You just buy fewer shares, because the size comes from the stop. Past 5%, I mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the stop by its distance from the buy. Up to 5% works, sized right.
questions.simple: True. 3.5% is inside the 5% we take, so you just buy fewer shares to fit it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3)
one web quote plus the card

questions.q: Kullamagi says a strong stock 'surfs' certain lines while it rests. Which ones?
questions.why: The rising 10- and 20-day. That's his picture: the stock rests, but it keeps riding its short averages up. On our charts those lines are the 9 and 20 EMA. A stock that holds them while it rests is still getting bought on every dip. He allows a toe of the 50-day once in a while. Once it starts closing under them, it's not surfing anymore.
questions.lesson_line: A good base rides its short averages up. On our chart, the 9 and 20 EMA.

wrong.The falling 50- and 200-day: Falling averages are a stock in trouble. He wants rising lines under a leader.
wrong.The 100- and 150-day: Far too slow. He's watching the short averages a leader rides.
wrong.The rising 50- and 100-day: Those are much slower lines. He names the rising 10- and 20-day.

questions.simple: The rising 10- and 20-day. A leader rides its short averages while it rests.

reasons: averages are the card's proposed reading, EMA or SMA unstated by the source

questions.q: How long does Kullamagi's consolidation usually run before the breakout?
choices: Two or three days at most
Six months or more, a long base
questions.why: About 2 weeks to 2 months, in his words. That's long enough for the stock to digest the run, and short enough that it's still a leader. Two or three days is just a pause, a flag. Six months is a different animal, the stock has lost its pace. And he never gives an exact count. It's a feel for the rest, and I read it the same way.
questions.lesson_line: Weeks, not days and not seasons. Judge the rest by its shape.

wrong.Two or three days at most: That's a quick pause, a flag. His rest takes longer, enough for the stock to really reset.
wrong.Six months or more, a long base: That long, the stock has lost its pace. His rest is weeks, not seasons.
wrong.Exactly 20 sessions, no less: He gives a range, not a count. Judge the rest by its shape, not by counting days.

questions.simple: About two weeks to two months. Long enough to digest the run, short enough to still be a leader.

reasons: A session count that is the card's own proposed number
Fixed before

questions.q: On our card, what is the deepest a base may be, high to low?
questions.why: 25%, measured from the consolidation high to its low, and no more than half of the prior move. A base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth.
questions.lesson_line: Shallow bases are stronger. Past 25% deep it is no longer this base.

wrong.15%: 15% is the A+ depth, not the limit. The cap is 25%.
wrong.10%: The card sets no 10% limit. The cap is 25%.
wrong.50%: That is far past the cap. The card allows 25%.

questions.simple: The base can be at most 25% deep, and the shallower it is the better.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (held)
the 25% cap is the card's proposed number and the owner has not ruled on it
a number that may change

questions.q: You've got a clean breakout lined up. Which reading on our market filter do you want before you really press it?
questions.why: Green. It's a bull-market trade. Breakouts work when the whole market is lifting leaders. Green means full risk for the grade and up to 10 positions. In Yellow I trade smaller and fewer. In Orange I only take my A+ ideas. Red is mostly cash. The filter is a guide, not a wall, but it tells you how hard to lean.
questions.lesson_line: Press breakouts in Green. Trade smaller as the reading weakens.

wrong.Yellow: Yellow means smaller and fewer. You can trade, but you don't press.
wrong.Orange: Orange is A+ setups only, and still with care. Not the time to lean on breakouts.
wrong.Red: Red is mostly cash. Breakouts have a hard time when the market's falling.

questions.simple: Green. Breakouts work best when the whole market is lifting leaders, so that's when you press.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
the card says Green only while the rulebook lets Yellow trade smaller

questions.q: A breakout on volume below its average doesn't count. Pass on it.
questions.why: False. Volume raises the grade, it's not a requirement. Big volume on the break is great to see, but quiet breaks work too. ISRG broke out of its flag on 0.7x volume and still worked. CPRI broke out on 0.8x and hit 3R in 5 days. So you still take the trigger. It just doesn't grade like your best idea.
questions.lesson_line: Volume raises the grade. It doesn't decide the trade.
questions.simple: False. Volume raises the grade, but a quiet breakout is still a breakout, and you still take it.

reasons: rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on

questions.q: A leader has built several bases on its way up. Which one would you rather buy?
choices: The first base after the move
questions.answer: The first base after the move
questions.why: The first one. It comes right after the stock showed you it can run, and fewer people trust it yet. Every base after that, the move is older and more holders are sitting on gains. Kell puts it simply: once you get two Base n' Breaks, you're late in the cycle. Late doesn't mean skip. It's a judgment call, and I'd just grade a later base lower and size it to match.
questions.lesson_line: Earlier in the run is better. Two bases in, you're getting late.

wrong.The third or fourth base: By then the move is old. Kell would tell you you're late in the cycle.
wrong.Whichever base is deepest: Deeper isn't better. A deep base means sellers had more say.
wrong.They're all the same: They're not. The later the base, the older the move and the more people already own it.

questions.simple: The first base after the move. Later bases come late in the run, so they grade lower.

reasons: The count rule is the card's own, built by analogy with Kell

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: ADR is the 20-day average of high over low, minus ___.
questions.why: 1. ADR is the 20-day average of high over low, minus 1. That gives the stock's average daily range as a fraction. The stop must be no wider than the ADR, and if it is wider we skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: ADR caps the stop. Know the stock's ADR before you buy.
questions.simple: ADR is each day's high divided by its low, averaged, minus 1, so it shows the usual daily swing.

reasons: rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on

questions.q: You bought at 161.59 with your stop at 158.95. Where's 3R?
questions.why: 169.51. Start with one R, your risk per share: 161.59 minus 158.95 is 2.64. Three of those is 7.92. Add that to your buy and you're at 169.51. Know that number before you're in. It's a yardstick, not a sell order. The first sell is a judgment, and HWM got to 3R in 7 days. Mark it on your chart so you can see the progress.
questions.lesson_line: Know where 3R sits before the open. Then let the trade work.
questions.simple: Risk per share times three, added to the buy. That's 169.51, a yardstick and not a sell order.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

wrong.$166.87: You added the three R to your stop, not your buy. R is always counted from the entry.
wrong.$164.23: That's only 1R. You need three of the 2.64.
wrong.$172.15: That's four R. Count again from the buy.

questions.q: The base topped at 64.40 and its low was 52.10. How far did it pull back from the high?
questions.why: 19.1%. The drop is 64.40 minus 52.10, which is 12.30. Divide that by the high, 64.40, and you get 19.1%. Always measure from the high, because that's where the pullback started. Then hold that number up against the run before it. A stock that ran hard can rest deeper and still be fine. Tighter is still better, and a tight base often hands you a closer stop.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a pullback from the high, in percent.
questions.simple: Take the drop and divide it by the high. 12.30 over 64.40 is 19.1 percent.

deeper.trap: Divide by the base high, not the low. Dividing by the low gives a bigger number and makes a decent base look worse than it is.

reasons: a computed key
the 25% cap named in the explanation is the card's proposed number

wrong.23.6%: You divided by the low. Measure from the high, where the pullback started.
wrong.12.3%: 12.30 is the dollar drop, not the percent. Divide it by the high.
wrong.80.9%: That's where the low sits as a share of the high. The pullback is the other 19.1%.

questions.q: You buy the break of the opening range in the first few minutes. Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
A few cents under the base's low
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the low of the day so far. Early in the session that's the opening range low. That's the level the break has to hold, so it's where you're wrong. It's also the tightest honest stop you'll get. I like it 1-3% away, and up to 5% is fine. Past 5%, I mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Early buy, early stop: a few cents under the LOD so far.

wrong.10% under the price you paid: Way too wide, and it ignores the chart. The stop goes where the break fails.
wrong.A few cents under the base's low: The base low can be far away. That's a wide stop, and it shrinks your size for no reason.
wrong.Under the 20-day average: An average isn't where this trade is wrong. Today's low is.

questions.simple: Under the low of the day so far, the opening range low. That's where the break fails.

deeper.trap: A stop under a moving average feels safer, but it's further away. You buy fewer shares and lose more when you're wrong. Past 5% from the buy, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (F62)
Opening-range version is the card's; the examples tested only the daily-chart trigger

questions.q: A leader clears its base high today. Its earnings report is two days away. Do you take the buy?
choices: No, too close to the report
questions.answer: No, too close to the report
questions.why: No. We don't open new buys in the 3 days before a report. One number can gap the stock right through your stop. Then the stop doesn't protect you, and you take whatever the open gives you. We only hold through a report when the trade's already up 5R, so there's cushion. Wait for the report, then look again.
questions.lesson_line: Check the earnings date before you check the chart.

wrong.Yes, the chart decides: The chart can't see the report coming. A gap through your stop doesn't care how clean the base was.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Size doesn't fix it. We skip new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Yes, then sell before earnings: That's a two-day trade with no room to work. Skip it and look again after the report.

questions.simple: No. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, so we don't buy just before one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Kullamagi wants the range 'tightening' into the breakout. What does that look like on the chart?
questions.why: The daily bars get smaller. Early in the base it swings around. Near the end the candles shrink and it barely moves. That's sellers drying up. Nobody's dumping, so it just sits there under the high. When it finally moves, it doesn't take much buying to push it through. Volume drying up often comes with it and raises the grade, but tight is about the range.
questions.lesson_line: Tight means small bars into the high. That's sellers running out.

wrong.Volume gets lighter each day: Volume drying up is nice to see. But tightening is about price, the size of the bars.
wrong.The base gets shallower overall: Depth is the whole base. Tightening is the last stretch, the bars shrinking into the high.
wrong.The 10 and 20-day come together: Averages pinching is how a Wedge Pop sets up. Here it's the price bars that tighten.

questions.simple: The bars get smaller near the end of the base. Sellers dry up, so it takes little buying to break out.

reasons: Only the card states the 5-session test
A number from the card's proposed criteria
Fixed before

questions.q: The breakout is ripping and it's already 6% over the trigger. It's strong enough that you can still buy it here.
questions.why: Nope, that's a chase. We never buy more than 4% over the buy point, however strong it looks. Your stop still goes under the low of the day, way back down there. So the distance to your stop grows and your shares shrink. And if it pulls back to the trigger, which is normal, you're sitting on a loss. Let it go. There's always another setup.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger is a chase. Let it go.
questions.simple: False. At 6% over the trigger you're chasing, and we never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% limit)

questions.q: Kullamagi trails what's left of his position with the 10- or 20-day moving average.
questions.why: That's his trail. After he sells some into strength, he rides the rest with the 10- or 20-day average. Ours is the same idea on our lines: the 9 EMA for a fast mover, the 20 EMA for a steadier one. A close under it sells what's left. The point is to let a big winner run without trying to guess the top.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength. Let the average sell the rest.
questions.simple: True. He rides the rest with the 10- or 20-day, and we do the same with the 9 or 20 EMA.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (E52, the trail)

questions.q: The EMA Crossback is bought as price trades above the prior session's high.
questions.why: True. Buyers show when price trades above the prior session's high on the first pullback into the rising averages. Kell says to always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in. The stop sits a few cents under the pullback's low.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for buyers: the Crossback buys over the prior session's high.
questions.simple: Yes. You wait for buyers to show by trading above the prior day's high, not just for a dip to the averages.

reasons: The trigger is the card's reading of Kell's confirmation

questions.q: Buy at market, or pass?
choices: Buy; this breakout is clearly real
Pass; it is over 4% above the high
Buy half now and half on a dip
Buy; it is under the 10% stretch limit
questions.answer: Pass; it is over 4% above the high
questions.why: Pass. The base high is 77.67 and we never buy more than 4% above the buy point. At 81.20 the stock is more than 4% above it. A real breakout bought that far past the trigger is a chase, so we skip it rather than scale in. The 10% limit above the 10-day average is a separate test.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger, skip it.

wrong.Buy; this breakout is clearly real: A real breakout bought more than 4% past the trigger is a chase.
wrong.Buy half now and half on a dip: No scaling. The price is past the limit and the plan skips it.
wrong.Buy; it is under the 10% stretch limit: The 10% line is a separate test for a long stretched above its 10-day. The 4% limit above the buy point still applies.

questions.story: The base high is 77.67. At 10:05 the stock trades at 81.20, and the trigger has long passed.
questions.simple: Pass, because the price is already more than 4% above the base high and that is chasing.

deeper.counter: Passing today is not a ban on the stock. A missed breakout that comes back to the breakout level may be bought as a new trade with its own trigger and stop. What the plan forbids is buying more than 4% above the buy point.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: Prior move 35.00 to 52.28. Base high 52.28, base low 45.00. What share of the move did it give back, in percent?
questions.why: The drop is 52.28 minus 45.00. The prior move is 52.28 minus 35.00. Divide the drop by the move to get 42.1%. The cap is no more than half of the prior move, so it passes.
questions.lesson_line: Give-back as a share of the move. Half is the most.
questions.simple: The base gave back 42.1 percent of the move, which is under half, so it passes the cap.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on
one cited fact only

wrong.13.9%: Divided the drop by the base high instead of the prior move.
wrong.16.2%: Divided the drop by the base low instead of the prior move.
wrong.57.9%: Found how much of the move it kept, not how much it gave back.

questions.q: Buy the break?
choices: No; a report is within 3 sessions
questions.answer: No; a report is within 3 sessions
questions.why: No. No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. Check the report date before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date first. A gap through the stop is not planned risk.

wrong.Yes; the volume confirms it: Volume does not move the earnings rule. No new buy in the 3 sessions before.
wrong.Yes, with half size: Half size does not fix a gap through the stop.

questions.story: A 14-session flag after a 41% run breaks out on 1.5x volume. The company reports after today's close.

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
choices: Lower it to give the trade room
Add more at the lower price
questions.why: Keep it. A close back inside the base in the lower third of its range is a failed breakout, and the stop decides.
questions.lesson_line: A failed close is a warning. The stop stays where it was.

wrong.Lower it to give the trade room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Add more at the lower price: No adds. One price, one stop.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 38.01 with the stop at 37.37. It closes at 37.60, back inside the base in the bottom third of its range.

questions.q: Buying inside the base, before it breaks out, is the normal way into this setup.
questions.why: False. We buy the trigger, the trade through the base high, while it happens. Buying early inside the base means you're guessing which day it goes. Kullamagi says he doesn't find anticipating as effective, and it takes more skill and experience. Wait for the break. It costs you a little price and saves you a lot of dead money in bases that never go.
questions.lesson_line: Let it break first. Then buy.
questions.simple: False. You wait for price to trade through the base high, because guessing early is harder and works less.

reasons: Our card is stricter than the originator, who allows anticipating

questions.q: A base that closes under its 50-day isn't the base Kullamagi buys anymore.
questions.why: Right. His base surfs the rising 10- and 20-day, and it might toe the 50-day once in a while. A close under the 50-day means it has lost all three lines. That's not a stock resting, that's a stock breaking down. Take it off the breakout list. If it repairs and builds a new base, it gets a fresh look.
questions.lesson_line: Losing the 50-day isn't resting. It's breaking down.
questions.simple: True. Closing under the 50-day means it lost its lines, so it's breaking down, not resting.

reasons: rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on

questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Pass, wait for a tighter one
Take it at half the size
Take it, stop moved up to 4%
questions.answer: Pass, wait for a tighter one
questions.why: Pass, mostly. I like 1-3%, 3.5% is good, and I'll go up to 5%. At 5.5% the stock has to fall a long way before you find out you're wrong. Don't fix it by pulling the stop up to 4%. That puts it in the noise above the real level, and a normal wiggle takes you out. Wait for a tighter trigger, like a higher low or a tight day to risk against.
questions.lesson_line: Past 5% to the stop, wait for a tighter trigger.

wrong.Take it at half the size: Smaller size doesn't fix a stop this far out. Past 5% we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
wrong.Take it, stop moved up to 4%: Never move the stop to make a trade fit. The real level is the low of the day.
wrong.Take it, 5.5% is close enough: Up to 5% is our line. Past it, we mostly wait.

questions.story: The base breaks out and you're about to buy. The low of the day sits 5.5% under your buy price.
questions.simple: Pass for now. The stop is too far away, so wait for a tighter trigger instead of forcing it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3)
the card still allows a stop over 3% with smaller size, a held decision
a number that may change

questions.q: Is this a flat base or a Qullamaggie breakout?
questions.why: Qullamaggie breakout. Look at the lows. A flat base sits in one box under a flat ceiling, and its lows don't climb. This one keeps making higher lows and tightens into the end. That's buyers stepping in sooner each time. Length doesn't split them, 25 sessions fits both. And you buy them the same way: through the high, stop under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lows. Rising lows into a tight finish, that's this breakout.

wrong.Flat base, it's long enough: Length doesn't decide it. A flat base is one flat box, and these lows keep rising.
wrong.Flat base, it tightens late: Both can tighten late. The rising lows are the tell.
wrong.Neither, it rested too long: 25 sessions is a normal rest, about five weeks. Nothing wrong with that.

questions.story: A leader rests 25 sessions after a big run. Its swing lows keep rising, and the range tightens at the end.
questions.simple: Rising lows make it the Qullamaggie breakout. A flat base is one flat box where the lows don't climb.

deeper.counter: Length doesn't tell them apart, since 25 sessions fits both. The shape of the lows does. Either way you buy the same: through the high at market, stop a few cents under the low of the day.

reasons: Compares against Flat Base and Bull Flag; the setup map is held (D-002)
Cut-offs come from the card's proposed criteria

questions.q: Bull Flag or Qullamaggie breakout?
choices: Neither; the drift is too short
Wedge Pop; it drifted after the run
questions.why: Bull Flag. A bull flag is a 3 to 15-session drift after a 20% pole, and this rest is five sessions. The Qullamaggie breakout rests 10 to 40 sessions, so under 10 sessions the rest is a flag. The 45% run alone does not decide it.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions. Under 10 is a flag.

wrong.Qullamaggie breakout; it ran up 45%: The run alone does not decide it. Under 10 sessions the rest is a flag.
wrong.Neither; the drift is too short: A short tight rest after a pole is a flag, a named setup of its own.
wrong.Wedge Pop; it drifted after the run: A Wedge Pop follows a Reversal Extension or a correction of 15% or more. This stock ran up and then drifted.

questions.story: A stock runs 45%, then drifts sideways for five sessions.
questions.simple: A five-session rest is shorter than 10 sessions, so it is a flag and not this breakout.

reasons: Compares against Bull Flag; the setup map is held (D-002)
Numbers from the card's proposed criteria

questions.q: What are you looking at here?
choices: Wedge Pop, from under the EMAs
A breakout, it cleared the range
A Base n' Break near its high
questions.answer: Wedge Pop, from under the EMAs
questions.why: A Wedge Pop. Most of its recent closes were under the 20 EMA, 11 of the last 15. So it wasn't resting above its lines. It was below them, and now it's coming back. Kullamagi's base surfs above the rising averages the whole way. Same push through the range, different story. A pop out of a downtrend is earlier and less proven than a leader breaking out, so you read it differently.
questions.lesson_line: A base that sat under the averages is a pop, not this breakout.

wrong.A breakout, it cleared the range: Clearing the range doesn't make it this breakout. That base rides above the rising 20-day the whole time.
wrong.A Base n' Break near its high: A Base n' Break holds the rising averages near the highs. This one lived under them.
wrong.An EMA Crossback to the 20: A Crossback is a dip to the line after a pop. This stock was under the line first.

questions.story: A stock spent 11 of its last 15 closes under its 20 EMA. Today it pushes through the top of its range.
questions.simple: It lived under its 20 EMA and is popping back up, so it's a Wedge Pop, not this breakout.

reasons: The 8-of-15 count is the card's own proposed number

questions.q: What do you call this buy?
questions.why: EMA Crossback. Kell calls it the first time the stock retests its averages after a strong move. That's this: a pop, then the first dip to the rising 20 EMA, then a turn up. You buy over the prior day's high, once buyers show you they're back. The breakout is a different trade. That's a new high out of a base, not a dip to a line.
questions.lesson_line: First dip to the line after a pop: a Crossback.

wrong.Qullamaggie breakout: That buys a new high out of a base. Here it's a dip to a line.
wrong.Base n' Break: That's a later pullback, after the Crossback. This one's the first dip.
wrong.Wedge Pop: The pop already happened. You're looking at the first pullback after it.

questions.story: A stock popped, then dipped to its rising 20 EMA for the first time and turned up. You buy over the prior day's high.
questions.simple: A first dip to the rising 20 EMA after a pop is an EMA Crossback. You buy over the prior high.

reasons: card criterion for Kell's crossback, constructed story

questions.q: What does the volume change?
choices: How wide your stop can be
questions.why: Just the grade. The 3.1x break grades higher, because big buyers are clearly in it. But the 0.7x break still counts. ISRG broke out on 0.7x and worked. CPRI went on 0.8x and hit 3R in 5 days. Your stop doesn't move either. It's still a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Volume moves the grade, not the verdict.

wrong.Whether it counts at all: Both count. Volume raises the grade, it's not a requirement.
wrong.How wide your stop can be: The stop comes from the low of the day, not from volume.
wrong.How tight the base was: Tight is about the bars in the base. The breakout day's volume doesn't change that.

questions.story: Two breakouts out of nearly the same base. One trades 0.7x its average volume on the day, the other 3.1x.
questions.simple: Only the grade. Heavy volume is a plus, but the quiet breakout still counts.

deeper.counter: Heavy volume is still welcome. The mistake is skipping a quiet breakout as if it didn't count. ISRG on 0.7x and CPRI on 0.8x both worked, though two examples don't make a rate.

reasons: the card's volume line is a proposed criterion
two examples, not a rate

questions.q: Which one do you like more?
choices: Day B, it waited for proof
questions.why: Day A. It broke early and held all day. Buyers took it through and nobody could push it back. Day B broke late and faded into the close. That tells you sellers were waiting up there. Both can work. I'd grade Day A higher and size it that way. There's no checklist for that, it's a read.
questions.lesson_line: Early and holding beats late and fading.

wrong.Day B, it waited for proof: A late break that closes off the high isn't proof. It's sellers leaning on it.
wrong.They're the same trade: Same trigger, different behavior. How it holds the break tells you a lot.
wrong.Neither, too hard to tell: You can read it. Early and holding beats late and fading.

questions.story: Two breakouts from similar bases. Day A breaks early through the opening-range high and holds. Day B breaks late and closes off the high.
questions.simple: Day A. It broke early and held, while Day B faded off the high, so sellers were waiting.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E50)
grade cues on the card are proposed

questions.q: How do you feel about that stop?
choices: Good, tight and inside its ADR
Too tight, it'll get shaken out
Tight enough to size up big
questions.answer: Good, tight and inside its ADR
questions.why: That's a good one. 1.7% is right in the 1-3% I like. And the stock moves 5.6% on an average day, so 1.7% is well inside its normal swing. Kullamagi caps his stop at the ADR, and this clears it easily. A tight stop means more shares for the same risk. It's not the whole grade, but it's a real plus.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop under the LOD is a real plus.

wrong.Too tight, it'll get shaken out: It's under the low of the day, where the break is wrong. That's not noise, that's the level.
wrong.Only the ADR matters here: Our line is distance from the buy. 1.7% looks great on that too.
wrong.Tight enough to size up big: A tight stop never licenses a monster position. A gap can jump right over it.

questions.story: You buy at 38.01 with the stop at 37.37. That stop sits 1.7% under the entry, and the stock's ADR is 5.6%.
questions.simple: Good stop. It's tight and well inside how much the stock moves in a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, E50)

questions.q: Where does that leave it?
choices: A leader, but not the best one
Not a leader, 82 is too low
A top leader, size it up
Out, a leader needs RS 90 plus
questions.answer: A leader, but not the best one
questions.why: It's a leader, just not the best one. 82 clears our line of 80. But a few names in its own group are stronger. When I have a choice, I want the strongest stock in the strongest group. So it's tradeable, and it grades lower than the group's leader. Check the others in the group before you settle on this one.
questions.lesson_line: Clear the RS line, then find the strongest one in the group.

wrong.Not a leader, 82 is too low: Our line is 80, so 82 is a leader.
wrong.A top leader, size it up: Mid-pack in its group isn't the top. I'd rather own the stronger names.
wrong.Out, a leader needs RS 90 plus: No, 80 is the line. A higher number is nicer, but it isn't required.

questions.story: A breakout candidate has an RS rating of 82. It sits mid-pack in its group, behind a few stronger names.
questions.simple: It qualifies at 82, but stronger names sit in its group, so it's not the one I'd want most.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (E50, grading is discretionary)
Grade cues are the card's proposed bands

questions.q: How do you handle this second break?
choices: An add to the first trade
Skip it, one trade per run
questions.why: It's a brand new trade. New trigger, new stop under the new low of the day, new size from that stop. The first trade is done and closed. We buy full size at one price with one stop. MSTR did this, flag after flag in one run. Each one gets planned on its own.
questions.lesson_line: Each flag in a run is its own trade.

wrong.An add to the first trade: You're flat. There's no first trade left to add to.
wrong.Skip it, one trade per run: A strong run can give you several flags. Each one is its own trade.
wrong.New trade, the old stop: The old stop belongs to the old trade. This one gets its own, under its own low.

questions.story: A stock broke out, ran, and you sold your shares. Weeks later it rests in a new flag in the same run. It breaks out again.
questions.simple: A new trade with its own stop and size. The first trade is over and closed.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

questions.q: Is that enough of a rest to trade the breakout?
questions.why: Yes. 10 sessions is two weeks, the short end of Kullamagi's 2 weeks to 2 months. A stock that just ran 47% and only gives back 14% while it rests is acting strong. Sellers had their chance and didn't do much. CRSP broke out on 3.1x volume, and 3R came in 1 day. Short rests in strong stocks can be the best ones.
questions.lesson_line: A short, calm rest after a big run still counts.

wrong.No, it needs 20 sessions: There's no count to hit. Two weeks of rest after a run like this is plenty.
wrong.No, 14% is too deep: Giving back 14% after a 47% run is a calm rest. That's strength.
wrong.Only if volume is huge: Volume raises the grade. It's not a requirement to take the break.

questions.story: The day before the break. After a 47% run, the stock has rested 10 sessions in a 14% band.
questions.simple: Yes. Two weeks of calm rest after a big run is short, but it counts, and it shows strength.

deeper.example: CRSP rested 10 sessions in a 14% band and broke out on 3.1x volume. CPRI broke out on 0.8x volume, and ISRG on 0.7x, and both still worked. That's why volume raises the grade instead of deciding the trade.

reasons: Example read from the research scan, not reviewed by the owner
Session and depth limits are the card's proposed numbers

questions.q: Does the depth rule this one out?
choices: Yes, it gave back too much
questions.why: No. 22% is on the deeper side, but this stock ran 71% first. Giving some of that back over 37 sessions is a normal rest. Depth is a judgment against the run, not a hard line. Tighter and shallower grades higher, so I'd size it a notch lower. AMD's buy was 15.98 with the stop at 15.20, 4.9% away. Wide, but inside our 5%.
questions.lesson_line: Judge depth against the run. Tighter grades higher.

wrong.Yes, anything over 15% is out: There's no fixed line like that. Judge the depth against the run before it.
wrong.No, deeper bases are better: Deeper isn't better. It means sellers had more say.
wrong.Yes, it gave back too much: After a 71% run, a 22% rest is normal. It held together and broke out.

questions.story: The day before the break. A 71% run, then a 37-session shelf 22% deep. The stock breaks out on 1.9x volume.
questions.simple: No. After a big run a deeper rest is normal, though a tighter one would grade higher.

deeper.trap: Depth isn't a pass or fail number. A stock that ran hard can rest deeper and still be fine. What I watch is whether the rest stays orderly, with the lows holding, and how the stop works out at the buy.

reasons: The 25% cap is proposed and the owner's own MRAM base ran deeper
Example read from the research scan

questions.q: Did you break a rule?
choices: No, the stop did its job
questions.answer: No, the stop did its job
questions.why: No. You followed the plan and the stop did its job. Your risk was 1.7%, and that's about what you lost. It got to 2.12R first, but no rule sells there. The first sell is a judgment, into a push a few days in. This was a late base, far along the yearly move, what Kell calls late in the cycle. Late bases grade lower. They don't get skipped.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out with the plan followed is a good loss.

wrong.Yes, you should've held on: The stop is the exit. Holding through it is how small losses get big.
wrong.Yes, should've sold at 2R: No rule sells at 2R. It only looks smart in hindsight.
wrong.No, but skip late bases: Late bases get a lower grade, not a ban. You can take them, just smaller.

questions.story: A 23-session base after a 32% run breaks out, far along the stock's yearly advance. You buy at 144.43 with the stop at 141.91. It reaches 2.12R, then stops you out on day 7.
questions.simple: No rule was broken. The stop worked, and a planned loss is part of trading this setup.

deeper.counter: Selling at 2R looks smart in hindsight. But no rule sells there, and the first sell is a judgment. The rule that mattered was the stop, and you followed it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B19)
late-base grading rests on a proposed card line
a number-heavy walk

questions.q: What should have kept you out?
choices: An ADR cap on the stop
questions.why: The earnings date. We don't buy in the 3 days before a report, and this one came that same evening. The next day gapped to a low of 112.91, right through the 119.75 stop. A stop can't protect you from a gap. The trade never traded above your buy. The chart was fine. The calendar wasn't. Check the date first, every time.
questions.lesson_line: The chart was fine. The calendar wasn't.

wrong.The 4% chase rule: You bought right at the break. Chasing wasn't the problem here.
wrong.An ADR cap on the stop: We judge stops by distance from the buy, and this one was fine. The report was the problem.
wrong.The 30-minute gap rule: That manages a gap after you own it. It doesn't keep you out of the buy.

questions.story: Prices are split-adjusted. A base breaks out. You buy at 123.06 with the stop at 119.75. The report comes that evening and the next day gaps below your stop.
questions.simple: The earnings date. We don't buy in the 3 days before a report, because a gap can jump the stop.

deeper.trap: This wasn't a normal stop-out. The next day gapped to 112.91, below the 119.75 stop, and the trade never traded above the entry. A stop only gets you out near your price when the stock actually trades there.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: What's that close telling you?
choices: Normal pause, add on the dip
questions.why: That breakout failed. It got through the high, then closed at the low of its range, back inside the base at 183.32. Buyers couldn't hold it, and sellers won the day. That close is your warning, and the stop is still your exit. QCOM's next low was 179.41, through the 183.06 stop, so the stop took you out. That's what it's there for.
questions.lesson_line: A close back inside the base at the low is a failed break.

wrong.Normal pause, add on the dip: Never add to a failing break. A close back in the base at the low is a warning.
wrong.A shakeout, lower your stop: The stop only moves up. Lowering it turns a small loss into a bigger one.
wrong.Nothing yet, check next week: The close already told you. Back inside the base at the low is a failed break.

questions.story: A 26-session base breaks out and you buy at 188.78 with the stop at 183.06. The day closes at the low of its range, back inside the base.
questions.simple: It failed. It closed back inside the base at the low, so your stop decides from here.

deeper.trap: The test is the close, not an intraday dip. A breakout that dips into the base and closes strong hasn't failed. This one closed at the low of its range, 183.32, back inside the base.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
failed-breakout test is a proposed card line

questions.q: What now?
choices: Out. Next trigger is a new trade
Lower the stop, the base is fine
Buy it back now, same stop
Hold, the dip was just a wick
questions.answer: Out. Next trigger is a new trade
questions.why: You're out. The low hit 59.83, under your 59.88 stop, so the broker order sold it. The base was valid and it failed anyway, for no reason you could see. That happens, and it's what the stop is for. If it sets up and triggers again, that's a new trade with its own stop and size. Don't buy it back just because you got stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Valid bases still fail. The stop pays for that.

wrong.Lower the stop, the base is fine: The stop only moves up. A good-looking base doesn't change that.
wrong.Buy it back now, same stop: That's revenge, not a trigger. Wait for the setup to trigger again.
wrong.Hold, the dip was just a wick: A real stop order already sold it when price traded under 59.88.

questions.story: A clean 16-session base after a 62% run breaks out. You buy at 62.10 with the stop at 59.88. The next day's low is 59.83.
questions.simple: You're out. Good bases still fail, and the stop is there for that, so wait for a new trigger.

deeper.trap: A valid setup can still fail. OXY passed every check and fell through the stop the next day. In our research scan, 28.9% reached 3R and 20.0% reached 5R before the stop, and 92% were stopped within 60 sessions. A stop-out is the cost of the setup, not proof you were wrong.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21, D41)

questions.q: That's shorter than Kullamagi's usual rest. How do you trade this break?
choices: Skip it, the rest is too short
questions.why: Same way you'd trade any of these. Eight sessions is under two weeks, short of Kullamagi's usual 2 weeks to 2 months. Call it a flag if you like. Honestly, a flag is a flag. What matters is the trigger and the stop. Set the alert at the high and buy at market as it trades through. Stop goes a few cents under the low of the day. A short, tight rest after a 39% run is strength, not a problem.
questions.lesson_line: A short rest is fine. Same trigger, same stop.

wrong.Skip it, the rest is too short: Short and tight after a big run is strength. There's no minimum count to hit.
wrong.Wait until it rests 10 sessions: There's no count to wait for. Judge the rest by its shape and buy the trigger when it comes.
wrong.Buy now, inside the rest: That's guessing. Kullamagi finds anticipating less effective. Wait for it to trade through the high.

questions.story: The day before the break. A 39% run, then the stock rests only 8 sessions sideways before it breaks out.
questions.simple: Same as any breakout. Buy as it trades through the high, stop under the low of the day.

deeper.trap: Eight sessions feels close to his range, and that's fine. Don't get stuck on the label. A flag and a short base buy the same way: through the high at market, stop a few cents under the low of the day.

reasons: near-miss logic rests on the dossier's single-gate reading
a rule number that may change

questions.q: What's wrong with this base?
choices: The run before it was too small
questions.why: The lows are falling. The last third bottomed at 34.89, under the first third's 36.52. That's a lower low inside the box. I want each dip to stop higher, buyers stepping in sooner. A lower low says the opposite: sellers are pushing it down. The 32% run and 19 sessions are fine. One bad tell is enough to pass.
questions.lesson_line: A lower low inside the box is a pass.

wrong.It's too long at 19 sessions: 19 sessions is a normal rest, under a month.
wrong.The run before it was too small: A 32% run is a real move. The lows are the problem.
