questions.q: A stock trades at $18 and averages 1,100,000 shares a day. About how many dollars change hands a day?
questions.why: $19.80 million. Price times shares: 18 times 1,100,000 is 19,800,000. That's just under our $20 million a day line. So even though the price is over $10, it fails. We want both: $10 or more, and $20 million a day. Under that it's hard to get in and out clean, and we don't even watch it.
questions.lesson_line: Price times shares. We want $20 million a day and $10 a share.
questions.simple: Price times shares is 19.8 million dollars a day, just short of the 20 million we need.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

wrong.$198.00 million: Slipped a decimal. 18 times 1,100,000 is 19.8 million.
wrong.$1.98 million: Slipped a decimal the other way.
wrong.$0.06 million: You divided the shares by the price. Multiply them.

questions.q: Can you take this one?
choices: No, 4 million shares is too few
questions.why: No. It fails the price test. We want $10 or more a share and $20 million a day. At $9.40 it's under $10. The dollar volume is fine, since 4 million shares at $9.40 is well over $20 million. But both have to pass. Clean base or not, it stays off the list.
questions.lesson_line: $10 a share and $20 million a day. Both.

wrong.Yes, it trades over $20 million: The dollar volume passes, but the price doesn't. Both have to.
wrong.Only at half size: Size doesn't fix a rule break. It's off the list.
wrong.No, 4 million shares is too few: The test is in dollars, and 4 million shares at $9.40 clears it easily.

questions.story: A leader trades at $9.40 on 4 million shares a day. Its 20-session base is clean and tight.
questions.simple: No. It's under 10 dollars a share, and both the price and the dollar volume have to pass.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Your stop math says 12,000 shares. The stock averages 800,000 shares a day. How many can you buy?
questions.why: 8,000. One percent of 800,000 is 8,000, and that's the most we'll own. The stop math said 12,000, but the volume cap is smaller, so it wins. The reason is getting out. Own more than 1% of a normal day's volume and selling in a hurry moves the price on you. Take the smaller number.
questions.lesson_line: Never own more than 1% of average daily volume.
questions.simple: 8,000. One percent of 800,000 is less than your stop math, so the smaller number wins.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

wrong.12,000 shares: That ignores the volume cap. The smaller number wins.
wrong.80,000 shares: That's a tenth of the day's volume, a slipped decimal.
wrong.800 shares: That's a tenth of a percent, a slipped decimal the other way.

questions.q: A stock trades triple its normal volume today, so you can size bigger off today's number.
questions.why: False. The cap is 1% of the average daily volume, not today's. One busy day doesn't change how easy it is to get out next week. Size off the average. If it's thin on a normal day, it's thin when you need to sell.
questions.lesson_line: Size to 1% of average volume, never today's.
questions.simple: False. You size off the average volume, because one busy day doesn't make it easier to get out later.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Our card calls which base depth the A+ depth?
choices: Half the prior move or less
questions.why: 15% deep or less. A consolidation 15% deep or less is the A+ depth on our card. The cap that decides whether a base counts at all is 25% or less, and also no more than half of the prior move. A base between 15% and 25% still counts but is not the A+ depth.
questions.lesson_line: A base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth.

wrong.25% deep or less: That is the cap every base must pass, not the A+ line.
wrong.Half the prior move or less: That is the second depth cap. A base can pass it and still not be A+ depth.
wrong.10% deep or less: The A+ depth is 15% or less. Ten percent is not a line on the card.

questions.simple: A base 15% deep or less is the A+ depth, while 25% is only the cap every base must pass.

reasons: Both depth lines are the card's proposed numbers
The 25% cap awaits an owner ruling

questions.q: Which do you like better?
choices: The 23% base, it has more room
questions.why: The 12% base. Same rest, same kind of run, but it gave back about half as much. Sellers had less say, and buyers held it up near the highs. A tighter base also tends to give you a closer stop, so more shares for the same risk. The 23% base can still work. I'd just grade it lower.
questions.lesson_line: Shallow and tight beats deep and loose.

wrong.The 23% base, it has more room: Deeper isn't more room. It's more damage to repair.
wrong.Same, depth doesn't matter: It does. Shallower and tighter grades higher.
wrong.Neither, both are too deep: Both are fine rests after a run. One is just cleaner.

questions.story: Two leaders break out of 15-session bases after similar runs. One base is 12% deep and the other is 23% deep.
questions.simple: The 12 percent base. It held closer to the highs, so it's the stronger rest.

reasons: rests on the criteria card, which the owner has not yet ruled on
grading is a judgment call

questions.q: Read the short lines the way Kell does. Is this one you take?
choices: Take it, base and volume are fine
Pass, the base is too short
Take it, flat lines mean tight
questions.why: I'd pass for now. The base and volume look fine, but the short lines haven't turned. The 9 is under the 20 and both are flat. Kell's line is blunt: with the 10-day EMA under the 20-day, there's no reason to be long. It's not one of our hard lines, it's a read. But on a breakout I want the 9 over a rising 20, with the stock riding them. Wait for the lines to turn up and give you a cleaner trigger.
questions.lesson_line: On the break, I want the 9 over a rising 20.

wrong.Take it, base and volume are fine: Volume raises the grade, it doesn't fix the lines. By Kell's read there's no reason to be long yet.
wrong.Pass, the base is too short: 20 sessions is a normal rest. The lines are the problem.
wrong.Take it, flat lines mean tight: Flat isn't tight. You want the lines rising under it.

questions.story: A leader breaks out of a 20-session base on good volume. It closes above its 50-day and 200-day, and the 50 is above the 200. Its 9 EMA sits just under its 20 EMA, and both are flat.
questions.simple: Pass for now. The 9 is still under the 20, so the short trend hasn't turned up.

deeper.counter: A long base and good volume don't rescue lines that haven't turned. Kell sees no reason to be long with the 10-day EMA under the 20-day. Wait for them to cross up.

reasons: Uses the 10/20 EMA pair held by D-021
Card rule on the breakout day
Fixed before

questions.q: What do you set up tonight?
choices: Alert at the high, plan written
A limit order resting at the high
An after-hours buy under the high
questions.answer: Alert at the high, plan written
questions.why: Set an alert at the base high and write the plan. Entry, stop and size, all down before the open. Tomorrow, when the alert hits, you buy at market. No thinking, no hesitating. A resting limit order can miss a fast break. Deciding after the open is how you end up chasing. And nothing gets bought after hours.
questions.lesson_line: Alert tonight. Market order tomorrow.

wrong.A limit order resting at the high: A fast break can jump your limit. We buy at market as it breaks.
wrong.An after-hours buy under the high: We don't buy outside regular hours, and under the high it hasn't triggered.
wrong.Nothing, decide after the open: Deciding live, while it moves, is how you end up chasing. Plan it tonight.

questions.story: It is 6 pm. A leader sits just under its base high, and you plan to buy the break tomorrow.
questions.simple: An alert at the base high and a written plan, so you buy at market the second it breaks.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58, D39)

questions.q: A leader breaks its level in pre-market. We buy it right there with a market order.
questions.why: False. We buy at market, but only in regular hours. Pre-market is thin, and prices can be all over the place. So the break waits for the open. If it opens more than 4% over the trigger, buying the open is a chase.
questions.lesson_line: Market orders, regular hours. Pre-market breaks wait.
questions.simple: False. We only buy in regular hours, so a pre-market break waits for the open.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: The 9 EMA sits at 50.00. Above what price is a long too stretched to buy?
questions.why: $55.00. Add 10% to the line: 50.00 times 1.1 is 55.00. We skip a long more than 10% over its 9 EMA. Up there you're buying far from support, and a normal pullback to the line costs you a lot. Mark that level before the open, and you'll know when it's gotten away from you.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% over the 9 EMA, skip it.
questions.simple: The 9 EMA plus 10 percent, so 55.00. Above that it's too far from support to buy.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

wrong.$45.00: That's 10% under the line. You want the line plus 10%.
wrong.$50.50: That's only 1% over. A slipped decimal.
wrong.$52.00: That's the chase idea, measured from a buy point. The stretch line is 10% over the 9 EMA.

questions.q: Buy it at the open, or pass?
choices: Buy, it's within 4% of the high
Buy half now, half on a dip
Pass, 3% over the high is too far
questions.why: Pass. It clears the chase check, since 3% over the base high is inside our 4%. But it fails the stretch check. 41.20 is more than 10% over its 9 EMA of 36.00. That's a stock far from its support. If it drifts back toward the line, that's a big pullback while you're holding it. Both checks have to pass.
questions.lesson_line: Two checks: under 4% past the high, under 10% over the 9 EMA.

wrong.Buy, it's within 4% of the high: That check passes, but the stretch check fails. Both apply.
wrong.Buy half now, half on a dip: We don't scale in. And a stock this stretched gets skipped.
wrong.Pass, 3% over the high is too far: 3% is inside our 4%, so the chase check passes. The stretch is what fails.

questions.story: The base high is 40.00. After a run, the stock opens at 41.20, just 3% over it. Its 9 EMA is 36.00.
questions.simple: Pass. It's close to the high, but more than 10 percent above its 9 EMA, so it's too stretched.

deeper.trap: Both lines must pass. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA. This open is 3% over the high but far over the EMA, so the second line fails.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
the key needs a little arithmetic

questions.q: Can you buy it?
choices: No, a missed break is gone
questions.why: Yes, as its own trade. Kullamagi says sometimes he buys the retrace. A break that comes back to the old base high and turns up through it gives you a new trigger. Your stop goes a few cents under that day's low, and the size comes from that stop. Monday's plan is gone. The 4% chase line still applies to the new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A missed break can come back with a new trigger.

wrong.Yes, but only half size: Missing the first move doesn't halve you. Size comes from the new stop.
wrong.No, a missed break is gone: Not always. A retrace to the level can give you a second shot.
wrong.Yes, with Monday's stop: Monday's stop belongs to a trade you never took. This one gets its own.

questions.story: A leader broke out Monday and you missed it. By Thursday it dips back to the old base high and turns up through it.
questions.simple: Yes. A pullback to the old high that turns up is a new trigger, with its own stop.

deeper.trap: A retrace buy is a second chance, not a bargain. It needs its own trigger, its own stop and the 4% limit, and the size comes from the new stop. Nothing from the first breakout carries over.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
the Kullamagi view comes from a reply in his comments

questions.q: You bought at 50.00 with the stop at 48.00. The stock gaps down, and the first 30-minute low is 45.80. How many R is that loss?
questions.why: 2.1R. One R is 50.00 minus 48.00, so 2.00 a share. The loss at that low is 50.00 minus 45.80, which is 4.20. Divide 4.20 by 2.00 and you get 2.1R. That's past our 2R ceiling, so you get out. When a gap blows through your stop, the first 30 minutes set the new stop. If that already costs you more than 2R, don't wait around.
questions.lesson_line: Past 2R in the first 30 minutes of a gap, you're out.
questions.simple: Lose 4.20 on a 2.00 risk and that's 2.1R, past 2R, so you get out.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

wrong.4.2R: 4.20 is the dollar loss a share. Divide it by the 2.00 of R.
wrong.25.0R: You divided the buy price by R, not the loss.

questions.q: Where's your stop now?
choices: Sell at the open, any price
questions.why: 47.20. The gap opened at 47.60, already under your 48.00 stop, so the old stop can't work. We let the first 30 minutes of a gap-down day decide. The low of that first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. At 47.20 the loss is still inside 2R, so you stay. If that low had pushed you past 2R, you'd be out.
questions.lesson_line: After a gap through your stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

wrong.48.00, the old stop stands: The stock opened under it. That stop can't fill there.
wrong.Sell at the open, any price: Give it 30 minutes. You only bail early if the loss is past 2R.
wrong.46.00, a stop 2R under the buy: 46.00 is the 2R ceiling, the point where you'd be out. It's not the new stop.

questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with the stop at 48.00. The stock gaps open at 47.60. The first 30-minute low is 47.20.
questions.simple: 47.20, the low of the first 30-minute bar. The gap jumped your old stop, so that bar sets the new one.

deeper.trap: Selling at the open feels safe, but it isn't how we handle a gap. Wait for the first 30-minute bar, then set the stop at its low. You get out early only if that low takes the loss past 2R of the original risk.

reasons: Rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 gap rule)
The 2R test is computed from the entry and old stop

questions.q: Is that good enough?
choices: No, place a real stop order
Partly, add an alert as backup
No, add the stop after a win
questions.answer: No, place a real stop order
questions.why: No. Put a real stop order in with the broker. A stop in your head doesn't fill when your internet drops, or when you freeze watching it fall. The order doesn't hesitate and doesn't hope. Set it right after the buy fills. An alert isn't an order either. It just tells you to do something.
questions.lesson_line: A real stop order, placed with the broker.

wrong.Yes, you're watching anyway: Watching isn't selling. People freeze, and connections drop.
wrong.Partly, add an alert as backup: An alert isn't an order. The stop sits with the broker.
wrong.No, add the stop after a win: The stop goes in right after the buy. It can't wait for anything.

questions.story: You will be at your screen all day. You plan to sell by hand if the stock falls to your stop.
questions.simple: No. A stop in your head isn't a stop, so place the real order with your broker.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: The trade dips close to your stop. You can lower the stop a little to give it room.
questions.why: False. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. You set it where the trade is wrong. Lowering it means risking more than you planned, on a trade that's already not working. The one exception is a gap through the stop, and that follows a fixed 30-minute rule, not a feeling.
questions.lesson_line: A stop moves up. It never widens.
questions.simple: False. The stop only moves up, and lowering it means risking more on a trade that isn't working.

deeper.trap: The pull is to lower it just this once when the trade dips near it. But moving it down or wider is how a planned loss turns into a big one. A gap is the only exception, and it follows a fixed 30-minute rule, not a mood.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Your breakout is working. Ideally, when do you move your stop up to breakeven?
questions.why: Somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell. Before 2R the stock needs room to breathe, and a breakeven stop just shakes you out of a good trade. Once it's up a few R, locking in a scratch makes sense. From there the trade can't turn into a loser. It's a judgment inside that window, not a fixed number.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R.

wrong.Between 0R and 1R: Way too early. Normal wiggles take you out at breakeven.
wrong.Between 10R and 20R: Far too late. By then you've risked giving back a big winner.
wrong.Between 6R and 10R: Later than you need. Move it somewhere from 2R to 5R.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. Early enough to protect it, late enough to let it breathe.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
the breakeven window is an ideal, not a hard rule

questions.q: You bought at 36.00 with the stop at 34.00. At what price can you start thinking about breakeven?
questions.why: $40.00. One R is 36.00 minus 34.00, so 2.00. The window opens at 2R. Two of those is 4.00, and 36.00 plus 4.00 is 40.00. From there you can move the stop up to your 36.00 entry. Anywhere from 2R to 5R works, or at your first sell.
questions.lesson_line: 2R over the buy opens the breakeven window.
questions.simple: Two times your risk, added to the buy. 36.00 plus 4.00 is 40.00.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

wrong.$38.00: You added the 2R to your stop, not your buy.

questions.q: You bought at 52.35 with your stop at 51.21. Where's 5R?
questions.why: $58.05. One R is 52.35 minus 51.21, which is 1.14. Five of those is 5.70. Add it to the buy: 52.35 plus 5.70 is 58.05. A tight stop like this puts 5R close by. Selling some into a push around 5 to 10R is often the best first sell. It's still your call on the day.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop puts 5R close. Know where it sits.
questions.simple: Risk per share times five, added to the buy. That's 58.05.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook

wrong.$56.91: You added the 5R to your stop, not your buy.
wrong.$46.65: You subtracted. 5R sits above the buy.

questions.q: How many shares do you have left to trail?
questions.why: 300. You started with 900. The first sale of 300 left 600. Today's 300 leaves 300. Those ride the trail now. A close under the 9 EMA sells them if it's a fast mover, under the 20 EMA if it's steadier. That's how you get paid along the way and still keep a piece for the big move.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some along the way. Trail what's left.

wrong.600 shares: That's what you had before today's sale.
wrong.450 shares: That's half of 900. You've sold 300 twice.
wrong.Zero, you sold it all: You'd be throwing away the piece that catches the big move. Trail what's left.

questions.story: You bought 900 shares and sold 300 of them on the way up. Today you sell another 300 by judgment, not by a fixed rule.
questions.simple: 300 left. 900 minus two sales of 300 is 300, and those ride the trail.

deeper.example: Walk it through. You hold 900 shares. 300 go first, leaving 600. Another 300 go next, leaving 300. That 300 trails: a close under the 9 EMA for a fast mover, or under the 20 EMA for a steadier one, sells it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, adjustable)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A gap above a trim level never forces a sale. Selling part at the open is your ___.
questions.why: Judgment. A gap above a trim level is not an automatic sell. Selling part at the open is one choice you may make, never a rule.
questions.lesson_line: Gap above a trim level: selling part at the open is a judgment.
questions.simple: A gap never forces a sale. Selling part at the open is a judgment call you may make or skip.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: What fits the plan at the open?
choices: Weigh selling some into the push
Sell a third, 3R is the rule
Sell the whole thing at the open
questions.answer: Weigh selling some into the push
questions.why: Weigh selling some into the push. It's day five, and it's gapping over 3R. That's the kind of push I like to sell into. But it's a judgment, not a rule. Some days I sell part into a big gap. Some days I let it run toward 5R or more. What you don't do is dump it all, or buy more into the gap. Sell some, trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: A gap up on day five is a push. Sell some by judgment.

wrong.Sell a third, 3R is the rule: 3R isn't a fixed sell. The first sell is your judgment.
wrong.Sell the whole thing at the open: You'd throw away the rest of a winner. Sell some, trail the rest.
wrong.Add shares, it gapped up: That's buying the gap, higher than you got in. A push like this is where you weigh selling.

questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 38.00, so 3R is 46.00. On the fifth day of the trade the stock opens at 47.50.
questions.simple: Think about selling some into the push. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Sell it now and free the money
questions.answer: Sell it now and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. 10 trading days in and it's only up 0.4R. Our time stop sells anything still under 1R after 10 days. The stop never got hit, but the trade isn't doing its job. That money can go to a stock that's actually moving. Breakeven isn't the answer either. That's for winners, somewhere between 2R and 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after 10 trading days, sell it.

wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven is for winners between 2R and 5R. This one's stuck at 0.4R.
wrong.Sell half, hold the rest: The time stop sells the trade, not half of it.
wrong.Hold, the stop isn't hit: The stop isn't the only exit. A stuck trade goes on the time stop.

questions.story: You bought a breakout 10 trading days ago. It has chopped sideways and is up 0.4R. The stop was never touched.
questions.simple: Sell it. A trade that's gone nowhere for 10 days is dead money, so free it up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Ten trading days in, the trade is up 1.5R. The time stop says you still have to sell it.
questions.why: False. The time stop only sells trades still under 1R after 10 days. At 1.5R it's working, so it stays. Your stop protects it, and when to sell some is your call.
questions.lesson_line: The time stop is for trades stuck under 1R.
questions.simple: False. It's over 1R, so it's working, and the time stop leaves it alone.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: What do you do with your position?
choices: Sell a big chunk into it
Hold it all for the 9 EMA
Trim a little, hold the rest
questions.answer: Sell a big chunk into it
questions.why: Sell a big chunk into it. Three straight up days, two overnight gaps, volume rising, and another gap today. That's a parabolic burst, the last fast leg of a move. Everyone's chasing it, and that's who you sell to. How much is your call, but a big part, not a token. Then the rest rides the trail.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run is where you sell, not where you add.

wrong.Add, it's working best now: It's never more stretched than this. You sell here, you don't add.
wrong.Hold it all for the 9 EMA: By the time it closes under the 9 EMA, you've given a lot back. Sell into the burst.
wrong.Trim a little, hold the rest: A climax deserves a big sale, not a token one.

questions.story: Your long has jumped three straight days with two overnight gaps up. Volume rose two days running, and today it gaps up again.
questions.simple: Sell a big chunk into the burst. A climax run is the time to sell into strength.

deeper.trap: Adding feels right because it's working best right now. But a climax is the moment the move is most stretched. Sell a big part into it. The rest still trails: a close under the 9 EMA for a fast mover, or under the 20 EMA for a steadier one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, B26)
a judgment call by the owner's own words

questions.q: Which of these is a sign of a parabolic burst?
choices: Volume shrinking on each up day
Three tight inside days in a row
A single gap up, then a quiet week
questions.why: Two straight overnight gap ups. A burst is the final fast leg, 3 to 5 days. You see three straight up days, two straight gaps up, wide bars, volume rising, and a gap up on the climax day. The more of those you see, the stronger the signal. Quiet tight days are the opposite. That's a stock resting, not bursting.
questions.lesson_line: A burst: gaps, wide bars, rising volume.

wrong.Volume shrinking on each up day: A burst runs on rising volume, not fading volume.
wrong.Three tight inside days in a row: That's a stock resting. A burst widens out.
wrong.A single gap up, then a quiet week: One gap and then calm isn't a burst. You want gap after gap.

questions.simple: Two straight gap ups. A burst is gaps, wide bars and rising volume, all at once.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: You're in a trade that's going nowhere, or going against you. What ends it?
choices: Either the stop or the time stop
A red close right after the buy
A hunch that the market is weak
Lowering the stop to wait it out
questions.answer: Either the stop or the time stop
questions.why: Your stop, or the time stop. Those are the two exits for a trade that isn't working. The stop takes you out if you're wrong. The time stop takes you out if it's still under 1R after 10 trading days. A red day, a gut feeling about the market, a scary headline: those aren't exits. They're how you sell good trades at the low.
questions.lesson_line: Two exits: the stop, or the time stop.

wrong.A hunch that the market is weak: A hunch isn't an exit. Your stop is.
wrong.A red close right after the buy: One red close is normal. The stop decides, not the color of the day.
wrong.Lowering the stop to wait it out: The stop only moves up. Lowering it just makes the loss bigger.

questions.simple: The stop if it's wrong, the time stop if it's stuck. Feelings aren't exits.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: How do you handle it?
choices: Hold, the stop is the exit
Sell at the open, news is bad
Lower the stop for the dip
Add on the dip, news is noise
questions.answer: Hold, the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. The stop is the exit, not the headline. The stock is still above your stop and still in profit. The plan you made before the buy already covers this. Selling on a downgrade swaps your rules for a mood. If it gaps through your stop, the 30-minute rule takes over. Until then, let the order do its job.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the exit. News is not.

wrong.Sell at the open, news is bad: The headline isn't your exit. The stop is, and it hasn't been hit.
wrong.Add on the dip, news is noise: You don't buy more on a dip. One price, one stop, and the stop is the plan.

questions.story: Day 6 after the buy. An analyst downgrade opens the stock down 2%. It is still above your stop and still in profit.
questions.simple: Hold. It's still above your stop, and a headline isn't an exit.

deeper.trap: A downgrade feels like new information, so selling or adding feels smart. But the plan was set before the buy, with a real stop order at the broker. If the stock gaps through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop, and you're out if the loss passes 2R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5)

questions.q: What do you want to see before a Wedge Pop?
choices: A drop, then price and EMAs tighten
A flat base riding above both the EMAs
A first dip into the rising 20 EMA
Three straight gap ups on volume
questions.answer: A drop, then price and EMAs tighten
questions.why: A drop, then a squeeze. The stock comes down, in a correction or a hard flush. Then it goes quiet under or against the 9 and 20 EMA while the two lines pinch together. That pinch is the wedge. When price pops through the top of it and closes over both lines, that's the trade. A cross of the lines by itself isn't the setup.

Yes, a burst down is the exception
